heading: A French address on the Coromandel coast
body: While the British East India Company was building its power around Madras, a rival trading company was doing the same eighty-five miles down the Coromandel coast. On 15 January 1674, the French East India Company's agent François Martin landed with a small party of men and began building a trading post at what would become Pondicherry, turning a small fishing settlement into a fortified port town over the following decades. Pondicherry became the capital of France's Indian territories, valued for the silk and cotton textiles — calicoes and muslins — produced by weavers in its hinterland, and it changed hands with the British more than once over the 18th century's Anglo-French wars before settling into French possession alongside three smaller enclaves: Karaikal, Yanam and Mahe, each separated from the others by British-ruled territory.

Pondicherry's most consequential moment as a French colonial capital came under Joseph François Dupleix, appointed Governor-General of French India in 1742. Dupleix pursued a strategy of inserting French-backed candidates onto contested local thrones across the Carnatic and the Deccan in exchange for territory and revenue, and for a period his forces made France the dominant European power over a large part of South India — a bid for empire that was ultimately checked by the British and reversed after his recall to France in 1754.

French rule persisted, on a much reduced and purely colonial footing, for two more centuries after that — right through the end of British rule in the rest of India in 1947. The four French enclaves were only transferred to India in stages: a referendum of elected representatives in October 1954 voted overwhelmingly for merger, and the territories passed to India de facto on 1 November 1954, administered from then on as Indian territory even though France had not yet legally ceded them. Full legal sovereignty followed much later — a treaty of cession was signed in 1956 but not ratified by the French parliament until 1962, with instruments of ratification exchanged in August of that year. The combined territory of Pondicherry, Karaikal, Yanam and Mahe was constituted as the Union Territory of Puducherry (as it is now officially spelled) from 1 July 1963.

The result is India's only former French colonial territory of any size, its four scattered enclaves still visibly distinct from the Tamil, Telugu and Malayalam-speaking regions around them — French-planned streets and churches in Puducherry town sitting alongside a much older Tamil temple town, a combination this map's entries for the region reflect.
